criteria.name: Introduction — Identifies ethical issues and broad links to engineering design; discusses the context of ethical issues in engineering organisations; identifies relevant stakeholders when considering the ethical issues.
criteria.reasoning: Introduction links Rachel’s shipping dilemma to engineering design and organisational competitive pressure, and names Rachel, company, chip supplier, health department and end-users. Ethical issues of public safety and professional responsibility are signposted.

evidence.quote: maintaining product quality safety while trying to succeed as a business in a competitive field
The relevant stakeholders in this scenario include Rachel, Rachel’s company, the chip contract company, the government health department

criteria.name: Balanced Discussion — Discusses objective arguments for and against decisions on the ethical issues; draws a conclusion on how stakeholders should make decisions about the issues.
criteria.reasoning: Balanced for/against arguments cover revenue, competition, jobs, harm, integrity and reputation, with a clear not-ship conclusion. Recommendations are mainly for Rachel/company, not several stakeholder groups, so very good not excellent.

evidence.quote: While there is some merit to shipping the products, such as economic benefits and maintaining a competitive advantage
the short-term benefit trade-off is greatly outweighed by the potential risks of harm to end-users

criteria.name: Compelling Argument that supports conclusion — The report forms a compelling argument that justifies the conclusion; the body follows a logical structure, with linked paragraphs and content ordered to support the argument; arguments demonstrate a systematic understanding of the ethical issues for all stakeholders.
criteria.reasoning: Structure moves from for/against to ethical path and conclusion; arguments support the recommendation. Stakeholder treatment is not fully systematic (chip supplier and health department are named but not deeply analysed), so very good.

evidence.quote: As seen by the points raised in the discussion, it is clear that Rachel faces a difficult decision.
the decision to Not Ship is certainly the most ethical path

criteria.name: Research and Evidence — Arguments are substantiated with adequate references and qualitative/quantitative evidence; research demonstrates a balanced, in-depth understanding of the topic.
criteria.reasoning: Uses EACE, NHS/HSSIB, Volkswagen and Apple cases, with some quantitative detail (hundreds of thousands of letters, billions in fines). Only four references, some incomplete, and not every claim is supported, so very good rather than excellent.

evidence.quote: In late 2023, the Health Services Safety Investigations Body (HSSIB) investigated a series ofIT system failures in NHS hospitals across England.
Volkswagen had installed “defeat devices” in a large amount of its diesel vehicles worldwide to manipulate emissions tests

criteria.name: Report Structure, Format and Language — The report includes appropriate sections serving their functions (abstract, introduction, body, and conclusion); maps, figures, tables, and visual elements are correctly used to support discussion; writing is grammatically correct, fluent, concise, easy to read and understand, and uses appropriate word choice; references are well-structured and appropriate, supporting the report’s motivations.
criteria.reasoning: Sections are present and prose is generally fluent, but there are typographical errors, no figures/tables, and references are few/incomplete (e.g. BBC entry lacks URL). This fits satisfactory rather than good.

Apple/CNBC reference supports iPhone release psychology, not clearly the claimed competitive-advantage argument.
No explicit decision framework or threshold for when a product with known defects may be shipped; recommendation is categorical refusal.

overall: Strong stakeholder-aware ethical analysis with clear not-ship recommendation and relevant case studies. Main gaps are no explicit decision rule for shipping known-defect products, limited/incomplete references, no visual elements, and typographical errors. Marks: C1 10, C2 8, C3 8, C4 8, C5 4.

feedback.summary: You wrote a strong stakeholder-aware ethical analysis with a clear not-ship recommendation and relevant case studies. Your INTRODUCTION and DISCUSSION identify key issues and stakeholders well. To reach the next level, add an explicit decision rule for shipping known-defect products, deepen analysis for all stakeholders, support asserted claims, complete references, and add visual elements with polished language.
next_steps: In 'The Most Ethical Path' and 'RECOMMENDATION', add an explicit decision framework or threshold for when a product with known defects may be shipped (for example severity, likelihood, consent and regulatory limits) and apply it to Rachel’s case; this addresses the partial R2 gap.

In 'DISCUSSION', support claims such as competitors shipping defective products and job loss with evidence, and analyse the chip supplier and health department as fully as Rachel and end-users; this strengthens C2, C3 and C4.

In 'References' and formatting, complete every entry (BBC URL, correct CNBC URL, consistent IEEE style), add at least one figure or table summarising stakeholders or decision criteria, and proofread headings and spelling; this targets C5 and R6.

criteria.C1: Your INTRODUCTION clearly links Rachel’s dilemma to engineering design and organisational competitive pressure, and names Rachel, the company, chip supplier, health department and end-users. This is Excellent. To consolidate, keep the stakeholder list explicit and signpost public safety and professional responsibility as you do; no higher rubric level exists for C1.
criteria.C2: Your 'The Most Ethical Path' gives balanced for/against arguments on revenue, competition, jobs, harm, integrity and reputation, leading to a clear not-ship conclusion. For Very good to Excellent, extend recommendations to several stakeholder groups (chip supplier, health department, end-users), not mainly Rachel/company, and add depth to each stakeholder’s decision.
criteria.C3: Your structure moves logically from for/against to ethical path and CONCLUSION, and your arguments support the not-ship recommendation. For Excellent, make stakeholder treatment systematic: analyse the chip supplier and health department as deeply as Rachel and end-users, and ensure every claim links explicitly to the conclusion.
criteria.C4: You use EACE, NHS/HSSIB, Volkswagen and Apple cases with some quantitative detail (letters, fines). For Excellent, add more references, complete them, and substantiate every claim—especially competitor behaviour and job loss—with qualitative and quantitative evidence. The Apple/CNBC source should clearly support the competitive-advantage point.
criteria.C5: Sections are present and prose is generally fluent, but C5 is Satisfactory: there are no figures/tables, references are few/incomplete (BBC lacks URL; CNBC malformed; IEEE uneven), and typographical errors reduce polish. For Good/Very good, add competent visual elements, complete and standardise references, and proofread headings and spelling.
